answer: I built GHZ states of 2, 3, 4 and 5 qubits. A GHZ state links all its qubits so they should all read 0 or all read 1 together. I sent the four circuits as one job with 100 shots each. I tested it first on sirius:mock (job 01a16059-cc10-7009-99aa-2317544494e2). Then I ran it once on the real sirius QPU (job 01a16059-fdb4-77cc-8884-25e7552221db). The mock returned all zeros, so it only proves the job is accepted and says nothing about the physics. The real job was billed 1.0 second, about 0.3 credits. On the real machine, the share of shots where all bits agreed was 0.94 for 2 qubits, 0.86 for 3, 0.80 for 4 and 0.79 for 5. A perfect machine would give 1.00 every time. The agreement falls as the state gets bigger. Each extra qubit needs more two-qubit gates, and every gate and measurement has a small chance of error. On sirius the qubits also talk through a central resonator, so extra moves add more steps. Those small errors add up, so the bigger the entangled state, the more shots land on mixed answers like 10 or 1011. The 4 and 5 qubit values (0.80 and 0.79) are close, and with 100 shots each the statistical error is about 4 percentage points, so the flattening at the end is within noise. The overall downward trend is clear. This shows that noise accumulates with circuit size, which is why entanglement is hard to keep on real hardware. Note that the all-agree fraction is only a lower-bound style check of GHZ quality. It does not test the phase coherence between the 00..0 and 11..1 parts.
